content: A malaria vaccine is urgently needed due to the significant global burden of mortality and morbidity caused by this disease. This review focuses on the outcomes of clinical trials involving blood-stage (asexual stage) malaria vaccines. While several vaccines are currently under development, only one, known as MSP/RESA or Combination B, has been evaluated in randomized controlled trials. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of blood-stage malaria vaccines in preventing infection, disease, and death. A comprehensive search was conducted in March 2006 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the Science Citation Index. Additional sources such as conference proceedings, reference lists, and direct communication with researchers and organizations were also utilized. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials that compared blood-stage vaccines (excluding SPf66) against Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, or P. ovale. These trials involved participants of any age who were exposed to a controlled malaria infection. The data from the trials were independently assessed by two authors, focusing on trial quality and outcomes. Dichotomous data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Five trials involving the MSP/RESA vaccine and a total of 217 participants were included in the review. All five trials reported on the safety of the vaccine, while only two provided data on its efficacy. No severe or systemic adverse effects were observed at antigen doses ranging from 13 to 15 µg per component (39 to 45 µg total). One small efficacy trial, which included 17 non-immune participants infected with blood-stage parasites, demonstrated no reduction or delay in parasite growth rates following artificial challenge. In a second efficacy trial conducted in Papua New Guinea, involving 120 children aged five to nine years, the vaccine did not reduce the incidence of clinical malaria episodes. However, it significantly reduced parasite density in children who had not received prior antimalarial treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. The vaccine showed a subtype-specific effect. Infections caused by the 3D7 subtype of MSP2 (the variant included in the vaccine) were significantly reduced (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.57; 719 participants). However, infections caused by the other major subtype, FC27, were not reduced (720 participants). In conclusion, the MSP/RESA (Combination B) vaccine demonstrates potential in reducing the severity of malaria episodes, particularly in a variant-specific manner. However, the interpretation of trial results is complicated by factors such as prior antimalarial treatment and the relatively small sample sizes of early trials. These findings suggest that blood-stage vaccines may have a role in malaria control and warrant further research and development.
